ReleaseLabel: dabbler-ai-orchestration extension 0.46.0 + docs/tutorials/hello-world.md (Set 106 'Hello-World Tutorial Simplification', walked in Session 4 of 4)
Notes:
AUTHORED IN SESSION 3, NOT YET WALKED. This checklist IS the acceptance test for this set. The operator quality bar forbids shipping untested step-by-step instructions, and docs/tutorials/hello-world.md is a brand-new document that replaced 1,968 lines across three retired ones -- every command, UI label and expected string in it was verified against shipped code by Session 1, but NOBODY HAS EVER PERFORMED IT END TO END. Session 4 runs this walk with the operator and fills in every Result / Feedback / Passes DURING the walk.

PASSES STARTS FALSE, AND THAT IS NOT A CLAIM OF FAILURE. Every item ships with Passes: false because nobody has walked it. False here means NOT YET WALKED; Session 4 flips each one to true at the moment it records that item's Result. This DELIBERATELY DEPARTS from the Set 078 and 103 exemplars, which shipped unwalked items as true, and the reason is that an acceptance artifact must fail CLOSED: a human or a script reading Passes on the old shape saw thirteen successes on a checklist whose own first sentence says NOT YET WALKED. An item with Passes: true and an empty Result is a contradiction, and the checklist gate now refuses it.

THE WALK DOUBLES AS THE VIDEO DRY RUN. Session 3 also authored nine OBS scene scripts under docs/tutorials/video/. Each walk below names the scene script that covers it, and you follow that script AS WRITTEN rather than improvising from the tutorial. A beat that cannot be performed as scripted is a DEFECT IN THE SCRIPT, not operator error -- record it in Feedback with the beat number. You are not recording video during this walk; you are proving the scripts are followable.

WALK ORDER MIRRORS THE TUTORIAL'S NATURAL ORDER, Part 1 through Part 6, with no reordering and no skipped steps inside the main path: Walk 1 = Part 1 (scene 1); Walk 2 = Part 2 (scene 2); Walk 3 = Part 3 (scene 3); Walk 4 = Part 4 steps 1-3 (scene 4 beats 1-9); Walk 5 = Part 4 steps 4-6 (scene 4 beats 10-14); Walk 6 = Part 4 steps 7-10 and the solo cutoff (scene 4 beats 15-21); Walk 7 = Part 5 steps 1-5 (scene 5 beats 1-8); Walk 8 = Part 5 step 6 (scene 5 beats 9-13); Walk 9 = Part 6 steps 1-3 (scene 6 beats 1-7); Walk 10 = Part 6's five-item final check (scene 6 beat 8). Walks 11 and 12 are DELIBERATELY OUT OF TUTORIAL ORDER and flagged as intentional: they are spot checks of the two alternate takes, which replace scenes already walked, so walking them in place would mean scaffolding the repository twice. Walk 13 is the whole-script attestation and can only run last.

THE SOLO CUTOFF IS A REAL CHECKPOINT. Parts 1-4 must read correctly for a one-person, one-module repository that will never add a second module (an operator requirement the spec names). Walk 6 ends on the tutorial's literal line 'Solo repositories can stop here.' -- at that moment, stop and ask yourself whether a solo reader who closed the page there would have a working, honest result. If not, that is a Major finding even though Parts 5-6 go on to work.

OPERATOR-SUPPLIED PRECONDITIONS, all named in the spec and ALL REQUIRED before Walk 1 begins -- if any is missing, STOP AND RESCHEDULE rather than run degraded, because a degraded walk re-creates the untested-instructions gap this set exists to close: (1) a GitHub account able to create a throwaway PUBLIC repository named hello-modules (public is what makes branch protection available on GitHub Free -- the tutorial's own caveat) and invite a collaborator; (2) a SECOND GitHub account or handle to play Sam, signed in in a separate browser profile; (3) a GitHub account holding an ACTIVE Copilot seat -- the seat must exist before the walk, but do NOT pre-authenticate the Copilot CLI and do NOT pre-install the Dabbler extension on the walk machine: Walk 1 installs and authenticates them, and a pre-provisioned machine cannot walk it; (4) a LOCAL BUILD of Session 2's 0.46.0 bump present as a .vsix, which Walk 1 installs INSTEAD of the Marketplace copy -- the Marketplace is still 0.45.0 and carries the OLD scaffolded templates, so walking on it would test the wrong CODEOWNERS and the wrong monorepo-ci.yml; that substitution is the ONE deliberate departure from a scene script in this whole walk -- scene 1 beat 2 tells a RECORDER to wait for the Marketplace rather than sideload, which is right for a video and wrong for this walk, whose entire job is to test 0.46.0 before the operator publishes it; (5) about two hours.

THE ONE-MACHINE STAGING TRAP, and it will wall Walk 8 if you skip it. You are playing two people. A second BROWSER PROFILE is not enough, because `gh auth login` writes ONE credential for the whole OS user -- not per folder and not per VS Code window -- and Dabbler: Open PR for this set runs `gh pr create`, so GitHub records the pull request's author as whoever `gh` is logged in as, NOT whoever wrote the commits. Leave `gh` signed in as Priya and every one of Sam's pull requests is authored by Priya, at which point Priya cannot approve them (GitHub refuses self-approval) and CODEOWNERS never requests her either (it never requests an author) -- Walks 8 and 9 both dead-end. Two people on two machines never hit this; you, on one, hit it every time. The fix is in Walk 7 step 2: log Sam's account into `gh` as a SECOND account, then `gh auth switch --user <handle>` before every pull-request action, checking `gh auth status` rather than trusting your memory. Walks 7, 8 and 9 each name the switch explicitly. This trap was found by the operator-ordered third-provider opinion after five same-provider verification rounds missed it.

PLATFORM: the literal commands below are the WINDOWS forms, because that is the walk machine (winget, .venv\Scripts\python.exe). The scene scripts carry the macOS/Linux equivalents at each beat -- npm install -g @github/copilot, brew install azure-cli, .venv/bin/python. On a non-Windows walk machine, take them from the scripts and record that you did.

WHAT AUTOMATION CANNOT CHECK, and why these walks exist: whether a stranger can FOLLOW the instructions. Every literal in the tutorial is machine-checked against shipped code (Session 1) and every literal shared between the tutorial and the scene scripts is machine-checked byte-identical (Session 3's s3-authoring-gates.md, 98/98 PASS). Neither gate can tell you that step 4 assumes something step 3 never established, that a wait is long enough to look broken, or that the reader is on the wrong branch by the time they get to the worktree. That is what a human walking it start to finish finds, and nothing else does.

PRODUCT DEFECTS ARE TRIAGED, NOT FIXED. This set ships no product behaviour change (spec non-goal). If a walk exposes a genuine product bug, record it in Feedback, apply an in-scope DOC workaround to the tutorial or the script, and name a follow-on set for the code fix. Do not change extension or router behaviour to make a walk pass.

Review.Subarea: Walk 1 - install and verify the four tools (scene 1)
Review.ItemLabel: A reader with none of the tools installed reaches a proven-working Copilot CLI and gh
Review.HumanAction:
Where you are: a machine with VS Code installed, NO folder open, the Dabbler extension NOT yet installed, and the Copilot CLI NOT yet signed in on this machine. Focus Assist on.
Follow docs/tutorials/video/scene-1-install-and-verify.md beats 1-9, which perform hello-world.md Part 1 steps 1-5. In order:
1. Install the Dabbler extension -- and here you DEPART from scene 1 beat 2 deliberately. That beat says not to RECORD until the Marketplace is at 0.46.0 or newer, because a video must show a path a viewer can follow. This is a walk, not a recording, and its whole purpose is to test 0.46.0's scaffolded templates BEFORE they are published, so install the local build: Extensions view > ... > Install from VSIX. Note the departure -- it is the only one in the walk.
2. Terminal > New Terminal, then run, one at a time:
   code --version
   python --version
3. Run:
   winget install GitHub.Copilot
4. Run copilot on its own and complete the sign-in prompt.
5. Run:
   copilot --version
6. Run the tutorial's smoke test verbatim:
   copilot -p "Write PI to 10 decimal places" --model claude-sonnet-4.6
7. Install the GitHub CLI from https://cli.github.com, then run gh auth login and gh auth status.
Review.Expectation:
Step 2: code --version prints three lines and the FIRST is 1.85.0 or higher; python --version prints 3.10 or higher. Step 3 ends in 'Successfully installed' (or reports the package is already installed -- also a pass). Step 5 prints a line beginning 'GitHub Copilot CLI ' followed by a version number. Step 6 prints pi to ten decimal places -- 3.1415926536 -- and exits without error; it must NOT print 'No authentication information found'. Step 7's gh auth status prints 'Logged in to github.com account <your-handle>' and a 'Token scopes:' line.
TUTORIAL-QUALITY CHECK, which is the real point of this walk: Part 1 must be followable with no prior Dabbler knowledge. Note in Feedback any step where you had to guess, and specifically whether the CLI-version-drift callout ('Expect copilot --version to drift past the pin; when it does, re-probe with Dabbler: Set Up Copilot Seat') reads as normal-and-expected rather than as an error you must fix now -- Session 1 found the operator's own seat already 6 patch versions past the pinned one, so a reader WILL hit this.
Review.ProgrammaticVerification: The literal command strings, the model alias claude-sonnet-4.6 and the smoke test's exit-0 behaviour were run live on this operator's seat during Session 1 and recorded in s1-runtime-unknowns.md ('Unknown 2 - The Copilot CLI version pin and the --model alias'), including the lockfile confirmation that claude-sonnet-4.6 has enablement = confirmed. The router's handling of this CLI's success and failure SHAPES is pinned by ai_router/tests/test_cli_transport.py and test_copilot_catalog.py against a fake transport; the live seat call here is what those fakes stand in for.

Review.Subarea: Walk 3 - scaffold, declare the greeter module, protect main (scene 3)
Review.ItemLabel: Build project structure scaffolds the repo and confirms the Copilot seat; New Module + Delete Module leave exactly one module named greeter
Review.HumanAction:
Where you are: hello-modules open in VS Code, one file, on main. The Dabbler icon is in the Activity Bar but has not been clicked.
Follow docs/tutorials/video/scene-3-dabbler-setup.md beats 1-13, which perform hello-world.md Part 3 steps 1-5:
1. Click the Dabbler AI Orchestration icon in the Activity Bar.
2. In section '1. Build project structure', leave Tier on Full, and under 'Provider access (how routed calls run)' select 'GitHub Copilot CLI seat'.
3. Click the Build project structure button and wait for BOTH progress notifications to finish (two to four minutes).
4. Ctrl+Shift+P > Dabbler: New Module. At 'New module (1/2): slug' type greeter. At 'New module (2/2): display title' type Greeter.
5. Ctrl+Shift+P > Dabbler: Delete Module. Pick Default. Confirm with the Delete Module button.
6. In the Explorer, delete the leftover folder docs/modules/default/.
7. Open docs/modules.yaml and edit the greeter entry so codeRoots is [services/greeter] exactly as the tutorial prints it. Save.
8. In the terminal: git add -A, then git commit -m "chore: scaffold Dabbler and declare the greeter module", then git push.
9. On GitHub: Settings > Branches > add a rule for main > turn on 'Require a pull request before merging' > leave the 'Require approvals' checkbox underneath it UNTICKED (that is zero approvals, and a solo reader needs it -- nobody else exists to approve them). If you are an admin, also enable the do-not-allow-bypass option.
Review.Expectation:
Step 1 shows a panel headed 'Getting Started' with section '1. Build project structure'. Step 2: selecting the Copilot option makes the 'Verification budget (USD, not-to-exceed)' box DISAPPEAR (it belongs to the direct-keys option). Step 3 shows a progress notification titled 'Building project structure...' and then a second titled 'Setting up the Copilot seat - probing the seat's models (about 1-2 minutes)...', and ends with TWO notifications: one beginning 'Project structure built (full tier):' and naming 'Default module scaffolded: 001-default-plan (plan) and 002-default-decomposition (decomposition)', and one beginning 'Copilot seat set up:' that names MORE THAN ONE provider and ends 'transport.profile: copilot-cli written to ai_router/router-config.yaml.' Step 4 opens a plan stub at docs/modules/greeter/project-plan.md and shows a notification naming '003-greeter-plan and 004-greeter-decomposition'. Step 5 shows a modal headed 'Delete module "default"?' whose detail includes 'Removed outright (2): 001-default-plan, 002-default-decomposition', and after confirming the Work Explorer shows ONE module group, Greeter, holding 003-greeter-plan and 004-greeter-decomposition. Step 8's push succeeds (it is the last direct push to main in the whole tutorial). Step 9 lists the main rule with 'Require a pull request before merging' on and 'Require approvals' UNTICKED. Record in Feedback whether the tutorial's wording matched the control you actually saw: GitHub's classic branch-protection UI expresses zero approvals by leaving that checkbox off rather than by offering 0 in a dropdown, and the tutorial was corrected to say so without anyone yet having walked it.
TUTORIAL-QUALITY CHECK: Part 3 step 2 explains WHY it is New Module + Delete Module rather than Rename Module. Confirm the numbering explanation ('Numbering starts at 003 because 001/002 were Default's') arrives before you wonder about it, and that step 3's 'no command does this for you' makes the codeRoots hand-edit feel deliberate rather than like a missing feature.
Review.ProgrammaticVerification: The exact behaviour of both writers against a REAL scaffolder-built fixture was established empirically in Session 1 and recorded in s1-runtime-unknowns.md ('Unknown 1'), including the finding that drove this branch: renameModule() does NOT follow the rename onto set folder names, planPath, or the plan file. The writers themselves are pinned by moduleAuthoring.test.ts, deleteModule.test.ts, renameModule.test.ts, modulesManifest.test.ts and gitScaffoldDefaultModule.test.ts; the seat-probe -> config-write flow by gitScaffoldSeatSetup.test.ts and copilotSeatSetup.test.ts on a fake spawner; the form's two-section shape and the Full-only transport sub-choice by gettingStartedHtml.test.ts and budgetSection.test.ts. The LIVE seat probe and the live GitHub settings page are what this walk adds.

Review.HumanAction:

Follow docs/tutorials/video/scene-4-first-module.md beats 10-14, which perform hello-world.md Part 4 steps 4-6. Substitute YOUR set's real name for 005-greeter-hello throughout:
1. Run, from the repository root:
   .venv\Scripts\python.exe -m ai_router.worktree open 005-greeter-hello
2. File > Open Folder... > the new hello-modules-worktrees/005-greeter-hello folder, in a NEW window.
3. In THAT window: click the Dabbler icon, left-click the set's row, open a terminal in that window, run copilot, paste the starter line, send. Wait.
4. Still in the worktree window, open .github/workflows/monorepo-ci.yml and edit the jobs: block to match the tutorial's printed YAML exactly.
5. git add .github/workflows/monorepo-ci.yml and commit it on the session branch.
Review.Expectation:
Step 1 prints exactly three lines: 'Worktree opened: <path>', 'Branch: session-set/005-greeter-hello (from main)', and 'Next: cd <path>'. Step 2's new window shows session-set/005-greeter-hello in the status bar. Step 3 creates services/greeter/greeter.py and a test beside it, runs the tests, verifies cross-provider, and commits to the session branch.
STEP 4 IS THE ONE TO WATCH. The tutorial claims this is an add-steps-only edit: 'the job is already named test, and it already runs on pull requests as well as on pushes to main.' Open the scaffolded file FIRST and confirm that claim is true of the file in front of you before you change anything. The job name (test), the step name (Build and test every module) and the on: block should need NO change. If you find yourself renaming the job, renaming the step, or editing on:, the tutorial and the scaffolded template have drifted -- record it as a Major.
TUTORIAL-QUALITY CHECK: Part 4 step 4 justifies the worktree as ISOLATION FROM MAIN, not as parallelism, and explicitly says the doc-only sets before it were fine on a branch in place. Confirm that distinction reads as a reason rather than an inconsistency.
Review.ProgrammaticVerification: The worktree CLI's canonical path, branch prefix, refusal cases and exact three-line output are pinned by ai_router/tests/test_worktree.py. The 'add steps only' claim is machine-checked by Session 3's s3-authoring-gates.md, which asserts the tutorial's YAML block is byte-identical to scene 4's AND that the fragments 'jobs:\n  test:', '- uses: actions/checkout@v4' and '- name: Build and test every module' are present in BOTH the scaffolded monorepo-ci.yml.template and the tutorial's target YAML, and that the template contains no 'if: github.event_name' gate to delete. Session 2's s2-green-on-empty-proof.md separately proves the scaffolded file is green on a repo with no modules. None of that proves a real GitHub runner accepts the adapted file -- that is Walk 6.

Review.Subarea: Walk 6 - the required check, the merge, Finalize, and the SOLO CUTOFF (scene 4 beats 15-21)
Review.ItemLabel: The first CI run happens, the PR merges, Finalize cleans up, and a solo reader can honestly stop here
Review.HumanAction:
Where you are: in the worktree window, on session-set/<your set>, with the code and the CI change committed.
Follow docs/tutorials/video/scene-4-first-module.md beats 15-21, which perform hello-world.md Part 4 steps 7-10 and its closing line:
1. In the worktree window: Ctrl+Shift+P > Dabbler: Open PR for this set. Accept the prefilled PR title. Read the dialog, click Push + create PR.
2. On GitHub, wait for the check named test to run and pass.
3. Merge the pull request.
4. Switch to the MAIN VS Code window. Ctrl+Shift+P > Dabbler: Finalize merged set. Read the dialog, click Finalize.
5. On GitHub: Settings > Branches > the main rule > turn on 'Require status checks to pass before merging' and select test. Save.
6. In the main window, from the repository root:
   python -m services.greeter.greeter
7. STOP. Read the tutorial's line 'Solo repositories can stop here.' and answer the question in the Expectation below before going on.
Review.Expectation:
Step 1's PR title prefills as 'Session set 005-greeter-hello' (your set's name) because the branch carries the session-set/ prefix -- unlike Walk 4, where it prefilled with the raw branch name. Step 2 shows a check named exactly 'test' -- the required-check name on GitHub IS the job name, which is why the template names the job test. Step 4 shows a modal headed "Finalize merged set 'session-set/005-greeter-hello'?" whose detail lists, IN ORDER, git pull --ff-only, git worktree remove <path>, git branch -d session-set/005-greeter-hello, and git fetch --prune; after confirming, a notification reads 'Merged set finalized.' followed by one line per step, the worktree folder is gone from disk, and the set sits in the Complete bucket. Step 6 prints exactly:
Hello, world!
STEP 7 IS A REAL CHECKPOINT, NOT A FORMALITY. A solo reader who closes the page here has a declared module, a plan, one completed AI-led set, a protected trunk and a green required check. Answer explicitly in Feedback: is anything they now have BROKEN or MISLEADING because they never read Parts 5-6? Named suspects to check: the docs/modules.yaml entry has no touches: key -- is that obviously fine? .github/CODEOWNERS is still entirely commented out -- does anything earlier imply it should not be? Required approvals is still 0 -- does the tutorial anywhere imply a solo repo is under-protected? A 'no' to any of those is a Major finding against Parts 1-4.
Review.ProgrammaticVerification: Finalize's step list, its ordering, its refusal to run from inside a worktree, its refusal on a dirty tree or a non-trunk checkout, and its use of -d rather than -D are pinned by gitWorkflow.test.ts against a fake process runner. Nothing programmatic covers the first live execution of the adapted workflow on a real GitHub runner, or GitHub accepting 'test' as a required status check -- both are first-time events in this walk.

Review.FunctionalArea: Part 5 - a teammate and a composing module
Review.Subarea: Walk 7 - invite Sam, declare app with touches, CODEOWNERS, approvals 0 -> 1 (scene 5 beats 1-8)
Review.ItemLabel: A second module that composes the first is declared and landed, and main now needs somebody else's approval
Review.HumanAction:
Where you are: greeter is on main, the test check is required, no worktrees open, main window on main and clean. Sam's account is signed in in a SEPARATE browser profile.
Follow docs/tutorials/video/scene-5-second-module.md beats 1-8, which perform hello-world.md Part 5 steps 1-5:
1. As Priya, on GitHub: Settings > Collaborators > Add people > Sam's handle > confirm. On a PERSONAL repository there is no role dropdown -- accepting the invitation is what grants push access. If you DO see a role picker you are on an organisation repository: choose Write, and record that the walk ran on an org repo.
2. As Sam: accept the invitation, clone the repository into a SECOND folder, open it in its own VS Code window, and run Ctrl+Shift+P > Dabbler: Install ai-router there. Then, in that window's terminal, add Sam to the GitHub CLI as a second account -- this is the one-machine staging fix, and Walks 8 and 9 dead-end without it:
   gh auth login          (sign in as SAM this time)
   gh auth status         (both accounts listed, one marked active)
3. As Priya: Ctrl+Shift+P > Dabbler: New Module, slug app, title App.
4. Edit the app entry in docs/modules.yaml to add codeRoots [services/app] AND touches: [greeter], exactly as the tutorial prints it. Save.
5. Open .github/CODEOWNERS, uncomment the two worked-example rule lines, and replace @priya-gh / @sam-gh with your and Sam's REAL GitHub usernames.
6. On GitHub: Settings > Branches > the main rule > TICK 'Require approvals' and set the count to 1. Save.
7. git switch -c authoring/app-module, git add -A, git commit -m "docs: declare the app module and route reviews", then make sure gh is acting as YOU -- gh auth switch --user <your-handle> followed by gh auth status -- and run Dabbler: Open PR for this set. THEN SWITCH TO SAM'S BROWSER PROFILE AND HAVE HIM APPROVE IT -- you cannot approve your own pull request and you raised approvals to 1 one step ago. Back as Priya: merge it, then git switch main && git pull --ff-only && git branch -d authoring/app-module
Review.Expectation:
Step 2's Install ai-router creates a .venv/ in Sam's clone -- it must NOT already be there, because .venv is git-ignored. Step 3 opens a plan stub at docs/modules/app/project-plan.md and its notification names app's two new lifecycle sets; the Work Explorer then shows TWO module groups, Greeter and App. Step 6 shows the main rule with 'Require approvals' ticked at 1. Step 2's gh auth status must list BOTH handles; if it lists one, the second login did not take and you must fix it before Walk 8.
STEP 7 IS THE FIRST TIME SOMEBODY ELSE'S DECISION IS LOAD-BEARING, and the ordering is deliberate: the tutorial raises approvals to 1 BEFORE landing this pull request, so the author is blocked on their own change. Before Sam approves, the Merge button must be DISABLED with a message that the branch requires an approving review; after he approves, it enables. If you were able to merge WITHOUT Sam, branch protection is not binding you -- you are an admin and the do-not-allow-bypass option from Walk 3 is off. Record which happened.
TUTORIAL-QUALITY CHECK: Part 5 step 3 explains why the tutorial asks for Priya's review BY HAND rather than relying on the CODEOWNERS rules it just added. Confirm that reads as an honest limitation rather than as the feature not working.
Review.ProgrammaticVerification: The manifest round-trip including touches:, and the Explorer's module grouping, are pinned by modulesManifest.test.ts, moduleAuthoring.test.ts, moduleTier.test.ts and visibleModules.test.ts, plus the Layer-3 module-tier.spec.ts rendering test.
